{{Short description|Relation between friction factor and Reynolds number}}
The '''Ergun equation''', derived by the [[Turkey|Turkish]] [[chemical engineer]] [[Sabri Ergun]] in 1952, expresses the friction factor in a [[packed bed|packed column]] as a function of the modified [[Reynolds number]].

==Equation==
<math display="block">f_p = \frac {150}{Gr_p}+1.75</math>

where:

* <math>f_p = \frac{\Delta p}{L} \frac{D_p}{\rho v_s^2} \left(\frac{\epsilon^3}{1-\epsilon}\right),</math> 
* <math>Gr_p = \frac{\rho v_s D_p}{(1-\epsilon)\mu} = \frac{Re}{(1-\epsilon)},</math>
* <math>Gr_p</math> is the modified Reynolds number,
* <math>f_p</math> is the packed bed [[Darcy–Weisbach equation|friction factor]],
* <math>\Delta p</math> is the [[pressure drop]] across the bed,
* <math>L</math> is the length of the bed (not the column),
* <math>D_p</math> is the equivalent spherical diameter of the packing,
* <math>\rho</math> is the [[density]] of [[fluid]],
* <math>\mu</math> is the [[dynamic viscosity]] of the fluid,
* <math>v_s</math> is the [[superficial velocity]] (i.e. the velocity that the fluid would have through the empty tube at the same volumetric flow rate),
* <math>\epsilon</math> is the void fraction ([[porosity]]) of the bed, and
* <math>Re</math> is the particle [[Reynolds Number]] (based on [[superficial velocity]]<ref name=obit>[https://web.archive.org/web/20221121071754/http://faculty.washington.edu/finlayso/Fluidized_Bed/FBR_Fluid_Mech/packed_beds_fbr.htm Ergun equation] on archive.org, originally from washington.edu site.</ref>)..

==Extension==
To calculate the pressure drop in a given reactor, the following equation may be deduced:

<math display="block">\Delta p = \frac{150\mu ~L}{D_p^2} ~\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2}{\epsilon^3}v_s + \frac{1.75~L~\rho}{D_p}~ \frac{(1-\epsilon)}{\epsilon^3}v_s|v_s|.</math>

This arrangement of the Ergun equation makes clear its close relationship to the simpler [[Kozeny-Carman equation]], which describes [[laminar flow]] of fluids across packed beds via the first term on the right hand side. On the continuum level, the second-order velocity term demonstrates that the Ergun equation also includes the pressure drop due to inertia, as described by the [[Darcy's law#Darcy–Forchheimer law|Darcy–Forchheimer equation]]. Specifically, the Ergun equation gives the following permeability <math>k</math> and inertial permeability <math>k_1</math> from the Darcy-Forchheimer law:
<math display="block">k = \frac{D_p^2}{150} ~\frac{\epsilon^3}{(1-\epsilon)^2},</math>
and 
<math display="block">k_1 = \frac{D_p}{1.75} ~\frac{\epsilon^3}{1-\epsilon}.</math>

The extension of the Ergun equation to [[fluidized bed]]s, where the solid particles flow with the fluid, is discussed by Akgiray and Saatçı (2001).
